title: Sudoku Solver
hints: You are given a partially filled 9x9 grid and must fill every empty cell with a digit 1-9 so that no digit repeats in any row, any column, or any of the nine 3x3 boxes. You modify the board in place, and exactly one valid completion exists.

Each empty cell's legal digits are limited by three groups at once: its row, its column, and its box. In the example, some cells have only one digit not already used by those groups. Also, choosing a digit for one cell immediately shrinks the options for every cell that shares a group with it.

The board is always 9x9, so input size is not the issue; the size of the search is. Trying all 9 digits in every empty cell blindly is about `9^k` combinations for `k` empty cells, which is hopeless. You need to throw away a bad partial assignment the moment it breaks a rule, instead of only checking full boards.

This is backtracking, a depth-first search over choices with undo. It fits because you make one decision per cell, can detect a conflict right away, and must be able to reverse a decision when it leads to a dead end.

Place a digit only if it is currently legal for that cell's row, column, and box, then recurse to the next empty cell. If some later cell has no legal digit, undo the most recent placement and try that cell's next digit. Checking legality must be `O(1)` so the search stays fast.

Keep three 9-entry lookup tables, each entry being a set of used digits: one per row, one per column, and one per box, where the box index is `(r / 3) * 3 + (c / 3)`. Also keep a list of the empty cell positions so the recursion can walk through them by index. Optionally, store each table entry as a 9-bit mask, so the free digits of a cell are the bits set in none of its row, column, or box masks.

Scan the board once, recording the given digits in the row, column, and box tables and collecting the empty cells.
Define a recursive step that takes an index into the empty-cell list.
If the index equals the list length, every cell is filled, so report success.
For the current cell, try each digit 1-9 that is unused in its row, column, and box.
Place the digit on the board, mark it in all three tables, and recurse on the next index.
If the recursion succeeds, return success right away; otherwise unmark the digit and restore the cell to '.'.
If no digit works, return failure so the caller backtracks.

The trickiest part is undoing correctly: on failure, remove the digit from all three tables and reset the cell. Also stop the search as soon as a full solution is found, or later backtracking will erase it. A board that starts completely filled should succeed immediately. A big speedup is to always branch next on the empty cell with the fewest legal digits (most constrained first). The worst-case time is exponential, roughly `O(9^k)` for `k` empty cells, but pruning makes it very fast on a 9x9 board. Extra space is `O(1)` for the fixed-size tables plus recursion depth up to 81.

review.summary: Your backtracking design is right, but two slips break it: the cell gets the column index instead of the candidate digit, and the cell is never cleared back to '.' when you undo a choice.
review.yourIdea: You record which digits are already used in each row, column and 3x3 box. Then you recursively find the first empty cell, try every digit that does not conflict, recurse, and undo the choice if the recursion fails. That is the standard constraint-tracking backtracking approach for this problem.

gaps.title: Undo must restore all state, including the board
gaps.explanation: Backtracking only works if undoing a choice puts the world back exactly as it was. You undo the three bitmaps on lines 25-27, but the board still holds the digit you tried. Your `solve` finds the next cell to fill by scanning for '.'. A cell that tried digits and then failed (line 30) keeps a stale non-'.' value. When an earlier cell switches to a new candidate and recurses, the scan skips that stale cell as if it were solved. Its digit is not even reflected in the bitmaps, so the search can 'succeed' with an invalid grid. Treat the board as part of the state: everything you change before recursing must be reverted after.

bugs.issue: You write `j + '0'`, which is the column index, instead of the digit `k` you just validated against the bitmaps.
When a candidate fails, the cell is not reset to empty. A deeper cell that exhausted its options stays filled with a stale digit.
bugs.fix: Along with clearing the bitmaps, restore the cell with `board[i][j] = '.';`.

counterexample.yours: board[0][2] = '2' (every empty cell in column 2 is written as '2', regardless of which digit k was chosen)
counterexample.why: Line 19 writes the column index j instead of the digit k. The bitmaps say one digit is placed while the board shows another, so the output is not a valid Sudoku.

complexity.time: Exponential in the worst case (up to 9^m for m empty cells), but heavily pruned. The 9x9 puzzles with a unique solution run in milliseconds. Each call also rescans the board in O(81).
complexity.space: O(81) recursion depth plus three 10x10 boolean tables.
complexity.verdict: Once the bugs are fixed this is the accepted approach and easily fits: the pruned search explores at most tens of thousands of nodes on typical inputs.

review.nudge: List everything you modify right before the recursive call on line 23. Then check that each one is reverted right after it. Also look closely at which variable holds the digit you are actually placing.
review.correctIdea: Keep used-digit tables for rows, columns and boxes. Find an empty cell and try each digit 1-9 not used in its row, column or box. Place it (board and tables), recurse, and if the recursion fails, undo both the tables and the board cell. Return true as soon as no empty cell remains. Because every change is fully reverted, the search explores valid partial grids only.
strengths: O(1) conflict checks using precomputed row/column/box tables instead of rescanning
Returning false right after exhausting candidates for an empty cell (line 30) is correct pruning

approach.oneLiner: Fill every '.' in a 9x9 grid with a digit 1-9 so that no digit repeats in any row, column or 3x3 box. Modify `board` in place; exactly one solution exists.
signals: "Fill the empty cells" so that every row, column and box stays valid → this is a constraint-satisfaction search: place a digit, check it, and undo it on failure (backtracking).
"It is guaranteed that the input board has only one solution" → the search can stop at the first complete fill, and you never need to report "no solution" for the whole board.
Each digit must appear "exactly once in each row/column/box" with digits 1-9 → the state of each row, column and box fits in 9 bits, so legality checks become O(1) bit operations.
`board.length == 9` is fixed → classical complexity in n is meaningless; what matters is how hard the search tree is pruned.
approach.constraints: The grid is fixed at 9x9 with up to 81 empty cells. Blind enumeration of 9^81 fillings is impossible, but backtracking that rejects a digit as soon as it conflicts explores only a tiny fraction of that space. So the target is a pruned search with O(1) legality checks, and ideally a smart choice of which cell to fill next.

thinking.q: What is the most naive way to solve this?
thinking.a: Try every digit in every empty cell and check the whole board at the end. With up to 81 blanks that is 9^81 boards, so you must detect conflicts while placing digits, not after.

Fill cells one at a time. Before placing digit `d` at `(r,c)`, check that `d` is not already in row `r`, column `c`, or box `(r/3)*3 + c/3`. If no digit fits, return false so the previous cell tries its next digit.

thinking.q: How do I make the check "is d legal here" cheap?
thinking.a: Rescanning the row, column and box costs 27 reads per check. Instead keep `rows[9]`, `cols[9]` and `boxes[9]` (booleans or 9-bit masks), filled once from the given digits. Then the check is three lookups, and placing or undoing a digit is three updates.

thinking.q: Does the order in which I fill cells matter?
thinking.a: Yes, a lot. Filling left-to-right may hit a cell with 7 options while another cell has only 1. Choosing the empty cell with the fewest legal digits (minimum remaining values) cuts the branching factor. A cell with 0 options fails immediately, and a cell with 1 option is forced.

thinking.q: How do I count a cell's candidates quickly?
thinking.a: With masks, the used digits at `(r,c)` are `rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[b]`. The free digits are the complement within 9 bits, and popcount gives how many there are. Scanning all empty cells for the minimum costs at most 81 cheap operations per search node.

approaches.name: Backtracking with full rescans
approaches.aha: The natural recursive idea is "find the next '.', try 1-9, recurse". The simplest validity check is to scan the row, the column and the 3x3 box directly on `board`.
approaches.idea: Walk the cells in row-major order. At an empty cell, try each digit 1-9 and check its row, column and box by scanning `board`. If the digit is legal, write it and recurse; if the recursion fails, reset the cell to '.' and try the next digit. Every complete filling reached this way is valid by construction, and the search tries every consistent partial assignment, so it must find the unique solution.
steps: Find the first cell containing '.' in row-major order; if there is none, return true.
For each digit d from '1' to '9', scan row r, column c and the box for d.
If d is not found, set board[r][c] = d and recurse.
If the recursion returns true, propagate true upward.
Otherwise restore board[r][c] = '.' and try the next digit.
If all 9 digits fail, return false.
approaches.time: O(9^m · 27) where m is the number of empty cells
approaches.complexity: The running time is dominated by the size of the search tree. Each node also pays a 27-cell scan per digit tried, plus a rescan to find the next empty cell. The only extra memory is the recursion stack, at most 81 frames deep.
approaches.tradeoff: It works on typical puzzles, but every legality check repeats work that a few counters could remember. Adversarial puzzles built against row-major order can make it explore millions of nodes.

pseudocode: function solve(board):  // returns true once every cell is filled legally
for r from 0 to 8:
for c from 0 to 8:
if board[r][c] = '.':  // first empty cell in row-major order
for d from '1' to '9':
if isValid(board, r, c, d):
board[r][c] ← d  // tentatively place d
if solve(board) = true:  // try to finish the rest of the board
return true  // success: propagate upward
board[r][c] ← '.'  // undo the choice, try the next digit
return false  // no digit fits here, so an earlier choice was wrong
return true  // no empty cell left: the board is solved
function isValid(board, r, c, d):
br ← 3 · (r div 3)  // top row of the 3x3 box
bc ← 3 · (c div 3)  // left column of the 3x3 box
for k from 0 to 8:
if board[r][k] = d: return false  // d already in row r
if board[k][c] = d: return false  // d already in column c
if board[br + k div 3][bc + k mod 3] = d: return false  // d already in the box
return true
function solveSudoku(board):
solve(board)  // fills board in place

parts.why: Each candidate digit is checked by rescanning its whole row, column and box on the board.

parts.cost: up to 9 branches per empty cell, depth m → at most 9^m search nodes
parts.why: Each of the m empty cells can try 9 digits, and every legal digit opens a new recursive branch.
Every call rescans from the top-left to find the next '.', which is a constant amount of work per search node.

time.sum: At most 9^m digit attempts × 27 checks each, plus ≤ 81 scan steps per call. That gives O(9^m · 27 + 9^m · 81) = O(9^m · 27) up to a constant factor; the exponential search tree dominates.
time.cases: Best case: a board where the first legal digit is always correct, giving about m · (81 + 9·27) steps. Worst case: a puzzle built so that many early guesses pass the local checks but fail deep in the search, which approaches the 9^m bound.
time.feel: m can be about 64. The 9^64 bound is astronomically large, but the row, column and box checks prune most branches, so typical LeetCode puzzles finish within milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds.

parts.why: Each frame fills exactly one empty cell and holds only r, c and d.
Only br, bc and k are stored; the scan reads the board directly.

space.sum: O(m) stack + O(1) locals = O(m), with m ≤ 81, so it is effectively constant.
space.note: The 9x9 board is the input and is modified in place, so it is not counted.

dryRun.input: Example 1's solved board with board[0][2] and board[0][3] blanked: row 0 = [5,3,.,.,7,8,9,1,2]; rows 1-8 are the expected output.

steps.explain: The scan passes (0,0)='5' and (0,1)='3', then finds (0,2)='.'. This is the first empty cell.
d='1': isValid scans and finds '1' in column 2 at row 6, so it returns false.
d='2' is rejected because column 2 has '2' at (1,2). d='3' is rejected because row 0 has '3' at (0,1).
d='4' appears nowhere in row 0, column 2 or the top-left box, so isValid returns true.
Line 8 recurses (depth 2). The new call rescans from (0,0) and finds the next empty cell at (0,3).
Digits '1' to '5' are all rejected: '1' is in column 3 at (1,3), '2' at (0,8), '3' at (0,1), '4' at (0,2) (the digit just placed) and '5' at (0,0). The trace stops on d='5'.
d='6' is absent from row 0, column 3 and the top-middle box, so it is legal.
Line 8 recurses (depth 3). This call scans all 81 cells, finds no '.', and returns true.
Back at depth 2, solve returned true, so this frame returns true without undoing the '6'.
Depth 1 also receives true and returns true, keeping the '4'.
solveSudoku finishes. The board now holds the filled grid, modified in place.

dryRun.result: Row 0 becomes [5,3,4,6,7,8,9,1,2], matching Example 1's output. Every digit was placed only after passing the row, column and box checks, and the search tried digits in order until a full legal board was reached.

approaches.name: Backtracking with row/col/box lookup tables
approaches.aha: The brute force rescans 27 cells to answer "is d used in this row, column or box?", yet that answer only changes when a digit is placed or removed. Store it instead.
approaches.idea: Precompute `rows[r][d]`, `cols[c][d]` and `boxes[b][d]` from the given digits, and collect the list of empty cells once. Recurse over that list by index. At each cell try digits whose three flags are all false; set the flags and the board cell, recurse, then clear them on backtrack. The flags always mirror the current board exactly, so the check is correct and costs O(1).
steps: Initialise three 9x9 boolean tables and an empty-cell list by scanning board once.
Define solve(i): if i equals the list length, return true.
Take cell (r,c) = empties[i] and compute b = (r/3)*3 + c/3.
For each d with rows[r][d], cols[c][d] and boxes[b][d] all false, mark the three flags and write d.
Recurse solve(i+1); return true if it succeeds.
Otherwise unmark the flags, reset the cell to '.' and continue; return false after the loop.
approaches.time: O(9^m) worst case, with O(1) work per tried digit
approaches.space: O(81) for tables plus O(m) recursion
approaches.complexity: Each search node now costs at most 9 constant-time checks, so the running time is just the number of nodes. The extra memory is the three 81-entry tables and the empty-cell list.
approaches.tradeoff: Each node is cheap, but the tree can still be huge because the fixed fill order ignores how constrained each cell is. One bad early guess in a loose cell can hide a contradiction for a long time.

approaches.name: Bitmask backtracking with fewest-candidates-first
approaches.aha: The Better version branches 9 ways on whatever cell comes next, even when another empty cell has only one legal digit. Always branching on the most constrained cell shrinks the tree dramatically.
approaches.idea: Store `rows[r]`, `cols[c]` and `boxes[b]` as 9-bit masks of used digits. At each step, scan the remaining empty cells and compute free = ~(rows[r]|cols[c]|boxes[b]) & 0x1FF. Pick the cell with the smallest popcount. If that count is 0, fail at once; if it is 1, the move is forced. Iterate over the set bits of free (lowbit trick), placing and undoing via XOR. This is still a complete search, so correctness holds, and it reaches dead ends as early as possible.
steps: Build the three masks and the empty-cell list from board.
If no empty cells remain, return true.
For each remaining empty cell, compute its free mask and keep the cell with the fewest set bits.
If that cell has zero candidates, return false.
For each set bit in its free mask, toggle the bit in its row, column and box masks, write the digit, and mark the cell filled.
Recurse; on success return true; otherwise toggle the bits back and restore '.'.
Return false when the candidates are exhausted.
approaches.time: Exponential worst case, but each node costs O(m) and in practice only a few hundred nodes are explored
approaches.complexity: Each node pays an O(m) ≤ 81 scan to choose a cell, and that scan is what makes the branching factor close to 1 on most steps. The memory is 27 masks, the empty list and the recursion stack.
approaches.tradeoff: Sudoku is NP-complete in general, so no polynomial guarantee exists. MRV trades an O(81) scan per node for a far smaller tree. Adding constraint propagation (naked or hidden singles) or Dancing Links can prune more, at the cost of more code.

mistakes: Using the wrong box index, for example r/3 + c/3 instead of (r/3)*3 + c/3. This merges different boxes, so valid digits get rejected or invalid ones accepted.
Forgetting to undo the row, column and box marks (or to reset the cell to '.') when backtracking. The tables then disagree with the board and the search wrongly prunes valid branches.
Continuing the loop after a recursive call returns true. Later trials overwrite the solved cells, so you must return immediately on success.
Comparing chars and ints carelessly: board holds '1'-'9', so the digit index is board[r][c] - '1', not board[r][c] itself.
edgeCases: {"case":"A board with very few givens (for example 17 clues)","why":"The search is deepest here, so the performance of fill-order heuristics matters most."}
{"case":"A board that is already complete","why":"The recursion must return true immediately without modifying anything."}
{"case":"A cell with exactly one candidate early on","why":"MRV should take it as a forced move. A fixed order might branch elsewhere first and waste work."}

{"case":"Puzzles designed against row-major order (the first row's solution is 987654321)","why":"These make the naive solver try many wrong digits in the first cells, which exposes slow implementations."}

takeaways: In backtracking, keep incremental state (sets or bitmasks) that you update on place and undo, so legality checks are O(1) instead of rescans.
Branch on the most constrained variable first (minimum remaining values); finding dead ends early shrinks the search tree enormously.
When the domain is tiny (digits 1-9), bitmasks give free set operations: union with OR, complement with a mask, iterating with lowbit, and counting with popcount.
When the input size is fixed, judge the algorithm by search-tree pruning, not by asymptotic growth in n.
